name: Copyright in the Digital Single Market Directive
evidence_rating: thin on the Directive itself; moderate causal evidence on predecessor national press publishers' rights (Spain, Germany); no measurement of Art. 17 effects
summary: The Commission promised that the Directive would help news publishers and other right holders license their content to online platforms, but set no measurable targets and has not yet evaluated it. Studies of earlier national publishers' rights found they raised little money and that when Google News left Spain, traffic to news sites fell by 8-14%. In France, Google paid only after EUR 750m in competition fines; the effect of the upload-filter rules (Art. 17) on creators, platforms and users has not been measured.

indicators.objective: The 2016 proposal has no financial-statement indicators; the memorandum only promised a review (Art. 30: no sooner than 7 June 2026). The impact assessment said indicators would be monitored every 2-3 years, but none has been published

indicators.indicator: Stronger bargaining position and more licensing revenue for press publishers
indicators.evidence: No systematic data on licence revenue. In France, Google first refused to pay; the competition authority fined it EUR 500m (2021) and EUR 250m (2024) for failing to negotiate in good faith / breaching commitments. Earlier national rights (Germany 2013, Spain 2014) produced little or no revenue; when Google News left Spain, traffic to news sites fell (8-14% in one study, about 10% for non-Google-News publishers in another), mostly hurting small outlets.
indicators.sources: Autorité de la concurrence 21-D-17, 24-D-03; Calzada & Gil 2020; Athey et al. 2021; JRC draft 2016/17

indicators.objective: Use of content by upload platforms (Art. 17)
indicators.indicator: Right holders better control and monetise their content; more licensing agreements; limited compliance costs for platforms
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The Commission's 2024 assessment of the start-up regime (Art. 17(6)) found 'limited evidence': almost no qualifying platforms identified, no platform answered the consultation. No study measures effects on licensing revenue, over-blocking or user uploads.

indicators.indicator: More legal certainty and lower rights-clearance costs for researchers, teachers and cultural heritage institutions

literature.citation: European Commission (2016), Impact Assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (executive summary SWD(2016) 302), SWD(2016) 301
literature.title: Impact Assessment on the modernisation of EU copyright rules (executive summary SWD(2016) 302)
literature.outcomes: licensing revenue; compliance costs; legal certainty
literature.headline: Qualitative only: press publishers' right to strengthen bargaining position without higher fees for services already licensing; upload-platform obligation to generate extra revenue for right holders with limited costs; costs could not be quantified overall for lack of data
literature.summary_plain: The Commission expected the new rules to help publishers and right holders license content to online platforms, but put no numbers on the gains.

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Assessment of the impact of Article 17(6) of Directive (EU) 2019/790, SWD(2024) 259 final (Council doc. 15441/24)
literature.title: Assessment of the impact of Article 17(6) of Directive (EU) 2019/790
literature.method: consultation of Member States and stakeholders
literature.headline: Limited evidence; very few Member States identified any platform under the start-up regime; no platform replied; right holders allege abuses without substantiation; 'difficult to draw at this stage any further conclusion'. Full Art. 17 review due no sooner than June 2026
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's first look at the lighter rules for upload start-ups found almost no evidence either way, partly because transposition was late.

literature.citation: Calzada & Gil (2020), What Do News Aggregators Do? Evidence from Google News in Spain and Germany, Marketing Science 39(1)
literature.title: What Do News Aggregators Do? Evidence from Google News in Spain and Germany
literature.method: difference-in-differences (Google News closure in Spain, Dec 2014; France and Italy as controls)
literature.headline: Spain's 2014 ancillary right led Google News to close; daily visits to Spanish news outlets fell 8-14% relative to France/Italy, with lower ad revenue; Germany's opt-in did not affect opted-out outlets overall but cut Axel Springer visits by 7%
literature.summary_plain: When Spain's publishers' right made Google News leave the country, visits to Spanish news sites fell by 8-14%, suggesting aggregators send readers to publishers rather than replace them.
literature.quality: causal (DiD); predecessor national laws, not Art. 15 itself

literature.citation: Athey, Mobius & Pal (2021), The Impact of Aggregators on Internet News Consumption, NBER Working Paper 28746
literature.title: The Impact of Aggregators on Internet News Consumption
literature.method: synthetic control (browsing data of 100,000+ users in Spain around Google News closure)
literature.headline: Google News shutdown cut overall news consumption of its users by about 20% and page views on other publishers by 10%; losses concentrated on small publishers
literature.summary_plain: After Google News closed in Spain, its users read about 20% less news and small publishers lost the most traffic.
literature.interested_party: Data from Microsoft users; Athey and Mobius affiliated with Microsoft Research

literature.citation: European Commission Joint Research Centre (2017), The economics of online news aggregation and neighbouring rights for news publishers (draft, released after access-to-documents request), JRC draft presented 2016, disclosed Dec 2017
literature.title: The economics of online news aggregation and neighbouring rights for news publishers (draft, released after access-to-documents request)
literature.headline: Aggregators increase traffic and ad revenue for newspapers; the market value of the German and Spanish rights 'so far remain zero'
literature.summary_plain: An internal Commission research paper, not published at the time, found that earlier national publishers' rights had raised no money and that news aggregators help publishers.

literature.citation: Autorité de la concurrence (France) (2024), Decisions 21-D-17 (EUR 500m fine, July 2021) and 24-D-03 (EUR 250m fine, March 2024) against Google on press publishers' related rights, French competition authority decisions
literature.title: Decisions 21-D-17 (EUR 500m fine, July 2021) and 24-D-03 (EUR 250m fine, March 2024) against Google on press publishers' related rights
literature.headline: Google fined EUR 500m for not negotiating in good faith with publishers after interim measures (2020), then EUR 250m for breaching four of seven commitments made in 2022
literature.summary_plain: France's competition authority had to fine Google twice (EUR 500m and EUR 250m) to make it negotiate payments to news publishers under the new right.

literature.citation: Doseva, Schmid-Petri, Schillmöller & Heckmann (2022), Uploaders' perceptions of the German implementation of the EU copyright reform and their preferences for copyright regulation, Internet Policy Review 11(4)
literature.title: Uploaders' perceptions of the German implementation of the EU copyright reform and their preferences for copyright regulation
literature.method: qualitative interviews (n=19) and content analysis of consultation comments (n=17)
literature.headline: Uploaders see state-mandated upload filters as restricting free expression and consider the German safeguards against filters ineffective in practice
literature.summary_plain: Interviews with German content creators found they see upload filters as a threat to free expression and doubt national safeguards work.
